speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Solicitor General if he has any report to make to the House on the disturbance which took place at Dorchester penitentiary today?

May 20, 1971

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: DORCHESTER-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON DISTURBANCE-DEPARTMENTAL INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, order has been restored since ten o'clock this morning. All prisoners have returned to their cells and the situation is under control.

subtopic: DORCHESTER-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON DISTURBANCE-DEPARTMENTAL INQUIRY
speechtext: How many prisoners have been injured at Dorchester and what is their condition?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: DORCHESTER-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON DISTURBANCE-DEPARTMENTAL INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, during the troubles, a number of prisoners tried to escape and the guards fired shotguns to warn them that they would be penalized. A few pellets hit two inmates who were carried to the hospital, taken care of, and sent back to their cells. A third inmate came out on his own from the place where a fight had apparently broken out among prisoners. This prisoner was carried to the hospital outside the penitentiary so as to be X-rayed to check the extent of his wounds.

subtopic: DORCHESTER-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON DISTURBANCE-DEPARTMENTAL INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Solicitor General if it is his intention to have a departmental inquiry into the reasons why prisoners from the assembly hall within the institution itself were wounded?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: DORCHESTER-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON DISTURBANCE-DEPARTMENTAL INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we will follow standing practice under the Penitentiary Act. The Commissioner will appoint a board of inquiry to investigate the causes of those riots.

subtopic: DORCHESTER-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON DISTURBANCE-DEPARTMENTAL INQUIRY

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there was no committee of inmates properly speaking, but some inmates handed us a document outlining their complaints. I could enumerate some of these, such as the fact that they had pork three times within the same week, that there are not enough classification offices, that salaries within the penitentiaries are inadequate, that clothing, and the type of clothing should be changed, that inmates do not get prompt replies to their applications for medical examinations, that they object to Parliament's having passed an act making probation compulsory.

speechtext: My question is for the Minister of Labour. speechtext: The point I made outside the House and inside the House, if the hon. member wants to read Hansard, was that if we extend seasonal benefits at a cost of $35 million we have no way of knowing precisely what portion of that $35 million will go to those unemployed people who are entitled to some extra help because, fortunately, we do not and never should include a means or needs test as one of the reasons for receiving unemployment insurance. speechtext:
that Bill C-246, respecting pilotage, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the objective of the bill is to provide the greatest possible degree of safety for ships which move through Canadian coastal and inland waters. In general, the recommendations made by the Royal Commission on Pilotage have been followed in the presentation of the act and while there is a considerable number of differences in regard to matters of detail, 36 of the 39 major recommendations made by the Royal Commission have been accepted.
By the establishment of four regional authorities, it is expected that the decentralization of the administration of pilotage services will be effected to the greatest possible degree. This is in keeping both with the recommendations of the Royal Commission and the wishes of the pilots and shipping interests of Canada as expressed over many years.
The bill replaces Part VI of the Canada Shipping Act which relates to pilotage in general and Part VIA which pertains specifically to pilotage in the Great Lakes. This bill is required because the accepted legislation, being of ancient origin, no longer corresponds to modem requirements. The Royal Commission found our present system
(Mr. Sharp.]
May 20, 1971

to be essentially sound but suggested new legislation to give it proper legal authority. In decentralizing the powers and functions of pilotage in Canada, essentially as recommended by the commission, the ministry will no longer be burdened with unnecessary involvement in matters relating to the day to day administrative operations of pilotage nor in the establishment of tariffs which, to an increasing degree, has resulted in increasing government subsidies.
The new bill envisages pilotage services operated to a large degree by regional authority rather than referring to a central authority. The regional authorities will operate with a great deal of autonomy in both regulatory and financial matters. It is anticipated that they will become financially self-sufficient and that subsidization will be reduced to a minimum, partly as a result of our over-all policy that the cost of government services should be met by the users. In place of the present 29 pilotage districts, there will be four pilotage regions.
The Atlantic Pilotage Authority will include all Canadian waters about the Atlantic provinces, plus the Bay of Chaleur between New Brunswick and Quebec.
The Laurentian Authority will include the St. Lawrence waterway from the northern entrance of the St. Lambert lock by Montreal to the waters of the gulf north of Cap d'Espoir in Quebec.
The Great Lakes will run from the northern entrance of the St. Lambert lock to all Canadian waters in and around Ontario and Manitoba, including Hudson Bay.
The Pacific Authority will cover the waters of British Columbia.
The four authorities will each have a chairman and a maximum of six members, appointed by the cabinet. The Chairman of an authority will be the chief executive officer and will be employed full time. In the larger regions, a full time vice chairman may be appointed. Their salaries will be set by order in council, as will be per diem rates for other members.
The pilotage authorities will have the objects of establishing, operating, maintaining and administering an efficient and economic pilotage service. They will be proprietary corporations under the provisions of the Financial Administration Act and will not be agents of Her Majesty.
The pilotage authorities will have powers to own land, buildings, boats and equipment, to borrow money and to make investments. They will be subject to audit by the Auditor General and will report annually to the minister. They may make by-laws for their internal management and shall file copies with the minister. Assets and liabilities of existing pilotage authorities will vest in the new authorities.
Pilotage authorities will establish compulsory pilotage areas and determine which ships are subject to the compulsory pilotage. In the compulsory pilotage areas, the person having the conduct of the ship must be either a licensed pilot or an officer of the ship holding a pilotage certificate.
Pilotage Act
All of the existing pilots' licences will continue in force and pilotage authorities will issue new licences to persons who qualify under the regulations. There will be periodic examinations of pilots in order to maintain their licences in force.
Pilotage authorities will either employ pilots on salary or, if the majority of pilots in a particular area so elect, may contract with a corporation of which the pilots are members for the services of pilots, and no person may exercise the privileges of a licence except under such conditions. A pilot's licence will not be valid unless he is an employee of the authority or a member or shareholder of such a pilot corporation. Pilots who become employees will be entitled to superannuation under the Public Service Superannuation Act and may count as prior service under that act the time they spent as licenced pilots under the Canada Shipping Act.
A pilot's licence may be suspended or cancelled when a pilot ceases to meet the qualifications set by regulation or when he violates certain disciplinary provisions. If the suspension exceeds 15 days, the pilot is entitled to a hearing, as he also is if an authority refuses to issue a licence. The hearing will be by the authority and may be held in public, and there is provision for an appeal to the minister. Appeals may also be made to the federal court if the appellant so desires.
Pilotage authorities will be empowered to make the regulations necessary to carry out their functions. Besides establishing compulsory pilotage they may prescribe classes of licences and pilotage certificates, the examination procedures for applicants for such licences and certificates, and limit the number of licences. These regulations are subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, and in the case of those establishing compulsory pilotage areas and prescribing qualifications for the holders of licences and pilotage certificates, prior notice must be published in the Canada Gazette. If any objection is made, the minister may direct that a hearing be held and may require the pilotage authority to vary the regulation before it is approved by order in council.
While pilotage authorities establish the qualifications respecting local knowledge, the Governor in Council will establish minimum qualifications respecting navigational certificates, sea time, age and health of applicants, and the examination respecting these matters. These regulations may also prescribe the forms of licences and certificates, the rules of procedure for hearings before a pilotage authority, and the establishment of compulsory pilotage areas where regional authorities fail to do so.
The charges for pilotage services will be established by regulations of the regional authorities with the approval of the Governor in Council. Every proposed tariff will be published in the Canada Gazette and any interested party may raise an objection with the Canadian Transport Commission. The commission will hold such investigations, including hearings, as it deems advisable, and pilotage authorities will be governed by its recommendations.

May 20. 1971
Pilotage Act
Because of the nature of pilotage in Canadian waters contiguous to waters of the United States, there will be a need for continuing consultation with the United States authorities in regard to the use of Canadian pilots in American waters and vice-versa. The bill provides for the promulgation of necessary regulations to continue the present Great Lakes pilotage arrangements and to make similar arrangements in other areas if necessary.
That, very briefly, is a summary of the objectives and the intent of the legislation now before the House. I may say that it is the result of exhaustive and lengthy consultation with various groups, including the pilots representing themselves, the shipping community and others who might conceivably be affected by this legislation.
I am aware that while, as I mentioned, there has been general agreement in principle with most of the provisions of this bill, certain reservations have been filed by interested parties, and I suggest that these can be discussed in detail when the bill is considered in committee. Certainly, I am disposed to hearing recommendations and to seeing what can be done to accommodate those who in the present circumstances feel that the bill should be strengthened or changed in certain respects.
At this point I might make reference to one matter in particular which I do know has concerned at least a small number of pilots and possibly a large group from whom I have not heard, and that is the possibility that in some instances their employment might be terminated prior to their having reached an age at which they could obtain full pension benefits. There is an ability within the legislation for such cases to be dealt with, and I certainly undertake here in the House to look at this particular provision and to ensure that there is no arbitrary abandonment of a man's work if the results or effects to him are very bad from a pension point of view.
Other representations have been passed along to me with regard to Bill C-246. Some of them are a reflection of the views of some of the more experienced pilots in the country, and to the extent that it is possible to implement these or to change the legislation in order to meet their suggestions, many of which I am sure are logical, we will be glad to consider them in committee.
I feel that what we have to do here is to bring the pilotage arrangements within Canada in line with modern conditions. As I mentioned in my earlier remarks, some of them are quite outdated. Indeed, one might even describe them as antiquated in terms of present circumstances. This is an effort on our part to meet the various representations that have been made over the years and also to comply with the proposals as set down in the royal commission report which was a very exhaustive, one might even say exhausting, exercise which has lasted for many years.
So with this I simply want to add that I will be appearing with the officials before the committee and at that time will deal with the specific matters that have been raised. Hopefully, we will arrive at a bill wh;ch can be reported back unanimously to the House in adequate time for it to take the place of the present more or less
ad hoc arrangements which expire, I believe, at the end of June.
May I at this point express my apologies to the opposition speakers who will be commenting on this matter and ask their indulgence for not being in my place during that period. The fact is that a delegation from Calgary came down here before I knew that the legislation was going to be discussed in the House at this particular time, and I will be with them for a few moments but will try to get back in time to hear the conclusion of this debate.

Mr. Speaker, we accept the minister's regrets. At least he is one minister who apologizes for not being here. I hope it is a good sign for the future.
In the latter part of the minister's remarks he made reference to guarantees to pilots. This gives me a chance at the beginning of my remarks to join him in mentioning this very important aspect of our marine activity, that is the pilots who serve as our navigators in and out of our harbours. This is a very noble profession, and in peace and wartime these pilots have made a great contribution to our country.
The legislation is based, as the minister said, on the Pilotage Commission report. The Pilotage Commission was established in 1962, and its report, as I said, forms the main basis for this legislation.
I just want to mention a member of the original commission Mr. R. K. Smith, who performed great service to this country in marine activities and in the Pilotage Commission. Mr. Smith had a very unique career. He was three times elected as a Member of Parliament and then, by some happening that I doubt could ever occur today, became a deputy minister of marine and fisheries, then Chairman of the National Harbours Board. Later, he was appointed to the Pilotage Commission. As I say, his was a unique career and he made a tremendous contribution to the country. He is a wonderful person, and his imprint is evident in a lot of the recommendations of the Pilotage report.
Again as the minister has said, this bill is designed to replace a part of the Canada Shipping Act, I think from section 323 on, dealing with pilotage. That part is all out-dated, and this bill is to meet new requirements. The old legisation was drafted to deal with conditions obtaining over a century ago. In the case of Saint John, in which I have some interest, I found that the people there had some pilotage requirements immediately after the Loyalists landed in 1783. This piece of legislation is one of those which Parliament amended from time to time and, as a result became very complicated. In fact, that applies to the whole of the Shipping Act. This is a point we should keep in mind during discussions in committee. Certainly, this is one bill that should not receive too much discussion now but should go to committee for detailed hearings.
The former pilotage authorities or local commissions were gradually usurped by the Department of Transport.

May 20, 1971

I notice a former minister of transport sitting in front of me, and he knows the difficulties with respect to regulations and routine work that the department had with the local pilotage commissions. The recommendations of the Royal Commission on Pilotage were quite clear in this respect. The Commission felt that the responsibility for pilotage should be withdrawn from the Department of Transport and placed under separate local authorities. A quick glance at the bill convinces me that this is only partially being done. There are various shades and degrees of bureaucracy, and its tentacles on power are still showing here. In any event, that was one of the recommendations and I want to go on record as saying that the removal of responsibility for pilotage from the department, so far as it is possible and practicable, is desirable. Of course, I agree that the Department of Transport, with its new re-organization, has to be a factor in anything we do.
The new legislation should be simple and clear. In it we should set out our intentions as clearly as possible, so that the public servants who may be involved with its administration will have a guide that will give them enough leeway to do what is desirable with respect to the day-to-day requirements and problems of the different regions that make up our pilotage service. We will have to state our intentions as definitely as we can in the legislation, but there will be many regulations involved. The problem will be to determine just how much control can be put in the legislation and how much should remain in the regulations. The Royal Commission on Pilotage said that the legislation should include precise, statutory definitions, and that principles and values should be enunciated. The new act should deal objectively also with the new organizational structure.
I return to the point which is the theme of my caution with respect to the legislation. I am not sure whether this is a direct quote, but Parliament should retain exclusive legislative control over those sections of the act which are of general application, and the pilotage authorities should deal with the rest of the regulations, particularly those of a local nature. The question is whether the bill fully meets this intention of the Pilotage Commission.
Clause 3 deals with the fitting of the legislation into the re-organization plan of the department, and implies the desirability of removing pilotage from the Department of Transport as far as possible. The four new pilotage commissions or authorities have been mentioned by the minister-the Atlantic, the Laurentian, the Great Lakes and the Pacific Pilotage Authority. There is some question as to where Churchill will fit, but that can be asked in committee. The commission recommended the creation of a greater number of authorities. This is a matter we should deal with. I am not saying that I object to a smaller number of authorities being created, but this will mean a need for more appointments to these authorities from the different areas, so that they will have on-the-spot knowledge of the navigational problems of the various areas.
The minister dealt with the question of the appointment of the chairmen of the various authorities and, in
Pilotage Act
accordance with that well known phrase, the Governor in Council will decide on the boundaries. This is something we may have to consider in committee.
Clause 4 deals with the Great Lakes Pilotage Authority which in some way is to be included in the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. We will want to know the reason for this. There may be administrative reasons, but I can see some difficulties since we know that the Seaway Authority has been losing money, and we would not want the Great Lakes Pilotage Authority to start out on a very pessimistic note.
Clause 6 deals with the question of appointments to the authorities. It does not state the conditions to be met by an appointee. Let us hope they will not be the usual political hacks, but people with a knowledge and experience of local navigation.

In clause 12 the language used in setting out the objectives of the authorities is not very colourful marine language. I would think we could improve on it. It talks high mindedly about the "safety of navigation," which is exactly what we have as an objective, but it appears to me that a landlubber wrote that phrase, or somebody in the department with a more technical problem in mind.
Later clauses deal with the matter of compulsory pilotage, the problem of the different types of licences, and the necessity to have pilots aboard ship. We should distinguish between pilotage licences and pilotage certificates. Anybody who has kicked around the waterfront knows that entirely different privileges are involved. I am not sure of the number of the clause which deals with regulations regarding United States pilots working in the seaway, but this and the clauses which deal with the matter of investigation are very important. We all know of the inquiry on the west coast into the case of a pilot who was under the weather during his working hours and although there are not many such examples, this is an extremely important matter.
Conditions governing licensing and suspension must be clearly stated in the act. Only Canadian cit.zens or landed immigrants are entitled to be licensed. If we are to encourage Canadians to go to sea and take up this aspect of marine activity, it is important that it be stated in the act as a definite requirement. Suspension of a licence is left in the hands of the chairman of one of the four authorities. My quick perusal discloses that the question of suspension and cancellation of licences by the pilotage commission is a very complicated one, and I think it should be dealt with extensively in committee.
Now, we come to the very important section dealing with the different tariffs for pilotage. The CTC is involved in this in some way which will be unfolded in committee. This is good or bad, depending on how you view the success of the Canadian Transport Commission, but at least there will be full publication and a formaliz-

ing of the tariff. The next section of the bill subjects the entire financial aspect to the scrutiny of the Auditor General. Of course, this is desirable but since public funds are not actually involved there will be no control by Parliament. The Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee will not approve this I am sure, and indeed I think most of us would have hoped for something more in the way of parliamentary control than the annual tabling of the report. 1 do not expect the minister to reply in detail now, but if I am on the wrong track entirely I am sure he will straighten me out. This legislation has been a long time in coming but it is very necessary. If we bring back a good bill from committee it will help navigation in and out of our ports and Canada will become a greater shipping nation. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the immense spectrum, the highly technical and complex activities that come under the umbrella of what is now described as the ministry of transportation is rather difficult for laymen to understand. I have always described it as one of the silent services which provides much of what makes it possible for Canadian citizens and their commerce to move with some degree of safety and regularity. Although I represent a coastal constituency and thus should perhaps know a little more of the current needs of the department than some other people, I confess my knowledge is rather fragmentary and rudimentary. So, it is with some diffidence that I rise to comment on this bill.
In his introductory statement, the minister largely confined himself to a description of the framework of the bill. He did not do much about putting it into perspective with the total picture that is emerging, I feel, about the changing requirements of the transportation of cargo by sea. Certainly, the operation of the pilotage services in the various parts of our country has an important relationship to the way in which that traffic moves. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that considering the leisurely pace of the Royal Commission on Pilotage it is rather startling to find this bill before us when we are being told that the final part of the pilotage report will not be available for some time.
If the introduction of the bill at this time means anything, I hope it means that there is recognition of a need
to act more quickly on some of these matters than has been the case in the past. As we consider this bill in committee, we may find that it is a companion to Bill C-2 which we discussed recently. The latter bill was designed to cope with the changing pattern of traffic and in particular with the use of high-powered vessels carrying larger cargoes which are in some cases, increasingly dangerous. There may be some interrelationship between the amendments which were made in that new part of the shipping act with respect to the bulk carriage of oil and other contaminant cargoes and the fact that the government has decided to introduce the legislation now being considered.
One thing I should like to say, in agreeing immediately that this bill should be read a second time and be referred to the committee, is that I hope there will not be any disposition on the part of those on the government side who may be responsible for the arrangements with respect to the committee to rush the bill through the committee. From my observations it seems that the bill, in some respects, has caught the pilots themselves off guard. Although they have been aware of the recommendations made by the royal commission, it is my impression that the abrupt manner in which the government has put forward these proposals on a matter that very closely affects their future as components of the marine work force of Canada has been a bit of a shock to them. The provisions of the bill will affect them directly as individuals and as groups of individuals.
I think most hon. members will agree that some of the basic rights of the people who have been within the pilotage services of the various regions of the country ought to be upheld, that their interests should be respected and that their careers should not in any way be unnecessarily interrupted or adversely affected by the proposed terms of this new bill. Having said that, I find myself inclined to agree with the recognition in the bill of the need to establish regional authorities which, in many respects, will be self-regulating and self-operating. The need for these stems from the fact that traffic on the Pacific coast-by that I mean the way it moves and operates and the components of it, whether made up of deep sea traffic or coastal trade-is very different from the kind of traffic that operates in the Great Lakes regions or on the Atlantic coast. So, the idea of establishing regional authorities seems a fairly sound approach. I gather that it arises in large measure from some of the recommendations of the royal commission.
I am not sure whether I understood correctly the observations of the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell); from my understanding of the bill, recognition has been given for the necessity of some kind of co-ordination between the ways these various pilotage authorities will operate. This co-ordination necessarily must be exercised as a result of appropriate action here, in Ottawa, under the authority of the governor in council. It appears to me at first blush-and this matter ought to be examined and discussed in committee-that the bill as

May 20, 1971

drafted preserves a fair balance between the idea of local and regional autonomy and the necessity of the exercise of essential co-ordination in order that we do not go off in all directions at once with respect to the uses and functions of pilots.
In several committees of this House recently, Mr. Speaker, there has been a good deal of discussion about what is required in order to secure adequate safety of navigation along our coasts, in waters leading to our ports, on the seaway and on the inland waters of Canada. One matter very much to the fore when committee consideration was being given to the unfortunate Arrow accident in Chedabucto Bay was the question of whether some of our basic ideas and basic legislative authorities in the field of navigation are adequate in this day and age. As most hon. members probably will know as a result of reading the press or of having read the proceedings before that committee, Dr. Patrick McTaggart-Cowan, who headed that task force, emphasized that ships on the seas approaching our coasts ought to be controlled in much the same way as aircraft are controlled at our airports or in our air corridors. He suggested that there ought to be parallel types of control procedures. Some people have questioned that concept and wondered whether such control procedures would necessarily be parallel. May I point out to the House that other witnesses quite independently, witnesses who were unaware of the position taken by Dr. McTaggart-Cowan, have said that this type of control is a necessary consequence of developments that are taking place.
This point of view was expressed the other day in the committee considering the dangers inherent in the proposed establishment of an oil tanker route from Alaska to Puget Sound, the Strait of Georgia, and then farther south. A suggestion has arisen that these vessels will be under direct traffic control through the use of radar and other electronic means, throughout their entire trip, or, at least, during certain parts of their journey. Certainly, there will be close control of navigation in the Straits of Juan de Fuca and up through Hecate Strait or Rosario channel and in the lower part of the Strait of Georgia. I say at once that this suggestion, to me, makes sense.
It is being pointed out in these discussions, however, that that concept challenges some very ancient maritime traditions under which the master of a vessel is a king of his own little domaine. One can recognize that in days of old when sailing vessels were out of communication with their home ports for extended periods, it was necessary for the master of the vessel to have this ancient authority. Under that concept, as I understand it, the pilot on a vessel serves, basically, in an advisory capacity to the master and the decisions remain in the master's hands. However, if the traffic control for vessels is to be somewhat similar to the kind of control exercised by an air controller operating from the control tower of an airport, it seems to me that we shall need to clarify not only the role of a master of the vessel and the question of who has ultimate power and authority, but also, in this context, the question of the role and authority of a pilot.
Pilotage Act
The bill makes provision for compulsory pilotage areas to be drawn by the different pilotage authorities. I agree with this. In fact, the concept of allowing masters of ships and those managing them to pay pilotage fees in lieu of taking on a pilot, thereby leaving inexperienced masters, inexperienced at least in local areas, in complete control of their vessel without benefit of advice, is archaic. In any realistic appraisal, certainly in view of the kind of discussion we have been having about the proposed tanker route on the west coast, there may be no option of that kind allowed.
If we think of the total pattern of marine traffic in a waterway such as the Strait of Juan de Fuca, we have to recognize that this kind of control, with its resultant elimination of the former authority of the master, may have to be applied to the master in charge of a large supertanker and also to masters in charge of other forms of traffic in difficult waters, be they towboats in the coastal area or freighters that carry dry cargo. I am sure hon. members agree that no matter how perfectly a supertanker is operated, if a freighter, inadequately manned in so far as expert navigational personnel are concerned, rams into it, the damage may be just as great as if the tanker were at fault.
I raise some of these questions because, in considering this bill, we should consider it in the total perspective with regard to the necessary requirements for the safe, normal and regular passage of marine traffic to and from our shores. I wish to emphasize that arrangements should be made so that this bill can receive adequate study by the committee. There should be a bit of a time lag in order to enable the pilots to properly assess the full implications of it as far as they are concerned. Steps should be taken to alert all who may be interested in the shipping field and, indeed, those who are concerned with the impact of a bill such as this on the marine ecology in the areas adjacent to our shores. I am glad the minister indicated there is some flexibility in his mind with regard to the details. When this bill is passed, it should be in a form which will make it a large part of a developing pattern to not only ensure free transport of our commerce, but also full protection of the ecology of our coastal areas.
In the past few days I have discovered that certain people who are very much concerned about what this House does really have not been made aware of some of the legislation we have passed. I do not know whether this is our fault. It may, in part, be theirs. Yesterday, someone whom I would have expected to be fully acquainted with the implications of the Shipping Act, which we dealt with earlier this session, had to admit he had not yet seen a copy of it. When I stated in a committee that this pilotage bill had been given first reading in the House, there was immediate interest. As a result, one of our messengers took steps to procure copies of this bill for distribution. The bill was eagerly seized upon by witnesses before that committee because they recognized it was something in which they were directly concerned.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, May 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lang that Bill C-238, an Act to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DETERMINATION OF PAYMENT FOR WHEAT-EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO FLAXSEED, RYE AND RAPESEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-238 is grouped with a number of grain bills which the government has brought before the House. Two of them are now receiving study by the Standing Committee on Agriculture. When one considers the plight of western grain farmers, it is interesting to note that a spokesman for the Canadian Wheat Board stated quite clearly this morning that there are 46,675 farmers in default on their cash advance borrowings from the wheat board. This gives one some idea of the plight of western farmers. To my mind this is a shocking figure. Farmers and people generally have the right to ask why.
It was also pointed out that the Wheat Board had carried out a deliberate policy of refraining from filling space available in commercial storage. There are some 170 million bushels less in storage this spring than was the case a year ago. I see the minister scurrying to look up figures. The figure I just gave was for the end of March-the amount varies from week to week. It can be said that farmers have delivered more wheat than they did last year. They delivered more this year because grain sales have been better than they were last year, but it remains true that the Wheat Board has carried out a program of refraining from filling elevators. What does this mean in terms of cash returns to farmers? It means we are not allowing farmers to sell as much grain as they otherwise might.
Now the minister is asking us to approve an amended Wheat Board act giving the Board jurisdiction over flax, rye, rapeseed and other things. The Wheat Board Act has been on the statute books now for 35 or 36 years. In essence, it has been a sacred cow. Western Members of Parliament and people generally have been afraid to criticize it because their remarks are immediately misinterpreted as meaning they are against the Wheat Board. I am for the Wheat Board. I think the Board has served a very useful purpose in western Canada. Nevertheless, I feel changes should be made. The act ought not to be a sacred cow; we should examine it. The direction of change should, in my opinion, be toward greater flexibility rather than greater rigidity. The act now before us places the farmer in an inflexible situation. The whole quota system has been altered in such a way as to make the farmers' position more rigid. It might be argued that since the government is handling grain sales through the Wheat Board it is in the best position to decide what farmers should deliver. Has the government allowed the Wheat Board to take all the grain for which it could find commercial storage? Is has not. These elevators could be filled. Instead, they are not being filled. This means less money for the farmer, less money for the machinery companies, for the grocery stores and for circulation in the economy generally.
Why has the government decided on this policy? I come back to the straightforward answer I suggested earlier. The government is deliberately trying to get rid of a lot of the small farmers. Some might say I am making no more than what amounts to a political statement-that nobody really believes it. Actually, though, this is Liberal policy as enunciated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in Winnipeg on June 2. He said on that occasion that a policy for small farms was necessary. Farmers would be kept on their land, but when they sold it, or moved, or retired, the land would have to go to a large scale farmer or else go back, to use the Prime Minister's phrase, into public hands. In other words, the government would own it. This is wrong. In my opinion, there will always be small farms. The government has the idea that once the operators of small farms have been got rid of the large scale farmers will be able to look after themselves, and no one in Ottawa will have to worry about them. This is a misleading line of thinking

May 20, 1971

because the large scale farmer of today becomes the operator of a small farm tomorrow, if we carry out a policy of this kind. Indeed, carrying this theory to the extreme, we could end up having only one farm. The Prime Minister likes to explain himself in that manner, by carrying things to extremes.
The minister in charge of the Wheat Board comes from western Canada, from the Province of Saskatchewan. He should know what wheat has meant to the economy of that province. He should know how short of money the farmers are in that province. But either he does not care about the people there, or he has no authority. I like to think it is the latter, because I believe the minister must care. He would not have run for election to Parliament if he had not cared a little for his constituency. On coming here, though, he realized that the policies had already been laid down by the bureaucracy in Ottawa. His job was only to carry them out, to administer them and to pilot the necessary bills through the House.
When the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) was in charge of the Wheat Board he used to say he had nothing to do with the affairs of the Board. The Wheat Board sold wheat. Today, quite evidently, the Board does not run its own affairs. A representative of the Board, an able gentleman, was asked a number of questions in the committee this morning to which he replied: "I cannot supply the answers." He could not supply the answers because he knew the Wheat Board is now being directed from Ottawa. This is wrong. There should be an amendment to the Wheat Board Act giving the farmers the right to elect a member to the Wheat Board. The Board is composed of five members. I would think that two, or better still three of them, should be elected, one from each of the Prairie provinces, so that the farmers would have a representative on the Board who would be responsible to them. This is one provision that should be in the act and is not. For too long the Wheat Board has been accused of not making sales, of being reluctant to make sales or of adjusting the price of grain, and this has caused anxiety and concern. If the farmers had a voice on the Canadian Wheat Board, the Wheat Board would then be directly in touch with the farmers whose grain they are selling, and any anxiety in the country would immediately be reflected in the decisions of the Board.
This bill is asking for permission to put rapeseed, flaxseed and rye under the control of the Canadian Wheat Board. In a press release recently-the minister is the greatest fellow for press releases-he said he had no intention of putting these crops under the full control of the Canadian Wheat Board, that he would consult the producers first. This reminds me of the famous Bill C-176. The minister had no intention of taking the cattlemen into the bill, so he told the cattlemen. He said he would eliminate them from the bill, but he has not done so yet. The minister has stated that he has no intention of ever creating a cattle marketing agency.
Do you really think, Mr. Speaker, that the minister would consult the producers of rapeseed before plac-
Canadian Wheat Board Act
ing rapeseed under the rigid control of the Canadian Wheat Board? Would he do that in view of the fact that he brought in this bill without even consulting them? The Western Producer carried an article recently in which it said that when the minister attended a meeting on the Prairies he was amazed to learn that the rapeseed growers did not come within the control of the Canadian Wheat Board. I see the minister is smiling at that, and I know he does not want me to read the article because it is slightly embarrassing. It goes on to say that the minister from Saskatoon put his head on the chopping block, and certainly I would not want to put his head on the chopping block.

speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board

speechtext: You have had it there so often. My head, I mean.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DETERMINATION OF PAYMENT FOR WHEAT-EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO FLAXSEED, RYE AND RAPESEED
speechtext:
I am sorry if I have left that impression because that is far from my mind. What I am asking is whether, as producers, we can believe that this government will consult us in view of the fact that it made no attempt to have prior consultation with the producers before introducing this bill to Parliament. The minister issues a press release in which he says these producers will never come under Canadian Wheat Board control or be included in the bill. This leads me to ask why they were put in the bill in the first place. This business of bringing in a piece of legislation, including provisions offering the producers, and then turning round and trying to reassure the producers that they will be unaffected by the bill just not good enough. Alarm has been expressed by our customers throughout the world at this measure. They want to retain their present flexible arrangement whereby they are able to buy rapeseed, in particular, without going through the Canadian Wheat Board. Rapeseed, flaxseed and rye are considered to be what are commonly known as cash crops; producers can grow these crops and sell them.
I should like to ask the minister whether it is his intention to pool the price of these grains when he does give control of them to the Canadian Wheat Board. He will probably consider the situation for some time, and if he does put them under the control of the Wheat Board perhaps he will pool the prices. I should like to know whether this is his intention, or whether he is doing this in order to make his grain stabilization program work and to enable him to keep accurate accounts of the cash received by the farmers.
I think it is a combination of both these two factors, but what is going to be the net result? Already alarm has been caused our customers. The farmers foresee it being slightly more difficult in the future to market their grains. For years we have had a surplus of wheat, and I think we should continue to have a surplus of wheat. I say this because we are entering a period of what I refer to as surge buying on the part of various countries. China and Russia have had crop failures I think three years out of the last ten and bought huge amounts of grain from Canada; we were fortunate to have that grain available. Under the program the minister is now carrying out, the amount of grain in commercial storage will be reduced.

May 20, 1971
Canadian Wheat Board Act
In that case, unless he is very careful, he will be unable to assure Russia, China, or Japan, which is buying in volume, that we will be able to make such deliveries.
This is the difficulty foreseen by the farmers in marketing their crops. I think we need a clear cut statement from the minister assuring us he is going to make every attempt, before the end of this crop year, to fill up all available commercial storage. If he puts forward the argument that by following this course difficulties will be created in the throughput of the grain handling system, that argument will not stand up. We have had our commercial storage facilities filled before. In various crop years in the past we have delivered huge amounts of grain to Russia and China during periods of near capacity grain storage in our commercial facilities, and there has been no difficulty with the throughput.
I submit that the first purpose of this legislation is to eliminate the operator of the small farm. The government thinks that the large scale farmer will then be able to look after himself and there will be less load on the government. The second purpose is to reduce government spending on agriculture. The government must have commercial storage either empty or practically empty so that it does not become involved in any major expenditure. Thirdly, the government wants to create a situation where it knows exactly what is being produced by any and all of the farmers. The government wants more control.
In a speech I made earlier in this House, on the subject of agriculture I said that what the government wanted was power, that the government wants to control every facet of our society, that the government is power hungry. It is not just content with being in office; the government wants power to control every facet of our society. That is what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) wanted when he introduced his marketing bill, though I do not think he wants it any more. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board is searching for power. He is trying to build up an empire for himself so as to control and to manipulate agricultural products. Instead of letting the Wheat Board run its own business, directions will be given from Ottawa. Instead of bringing in a bill to allow the farmer to have some representation on the Wheat Board, there is to be more rigidity in the system.
If one carefully studied the agricultural situation during the past number of years, one would realize that the most successful farmer has been the farmer who has been most flexible, who has been able to shift his energy from one phase of the industry to another and therefore meet the market as it develops. The rigidity this government is bringing to the agricultural scene is wrong. It will prohibit the flexibility required in an individual farmer's operation. In my opinion, the whole concept goes back to the question of supply management. This government is firmly committed to supply management. The Operation Lift which the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board brought in last year was a direct
attempt at supply management. Now, the minister throws out his chest and says that it was pretty successful because the amount of wheat was reduced. Yes, he reduced the amount of wheat because he introduced a program whereby if a farmer did seed wheat he could not deliver it. That was the way the quota system worked.
Canada is a small country in population but a country which is large in resources and ability. For a long time the farmers have listened to the government experts, the bureaucrats, say that greater efficiency is required in the agricultural industry. The farmers need more effectiveness from the government rather than greater efficiency. Now, the minister states that supply management will give this. Canada is a country which has the ability to produce something in the neighbourhood of less than 10 per cent of the world's wheat production and yet it has nearly 50 per cent of the world's surplus. We need sales. If we say we cannot sell it then, in effect, we are saying that all the people in the world go to bed with no more desire to have a greater supply of food. We all know this is wrong. We know there are many people throughout the world who require more food. To me, the concept of supply management is an example of negative thinking. We are opting out of competition throughout the world. We should be doing the direct opposite.
The Canadian Wheat Board should be adopting a system of selling agencies or if the Canadian Wheat Board does not wish to do this the government should do so. I asked the former chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board about this and he said he felt the board should be involved in a pricing, pooling and orderly marketing system. However, he would prefer not to have selling agencies under the board because the board must be impartial and must treat all the various selling agencies alike. If that is the opinion of the board, then the Canadian government should be giving financial assistance to the newly established selling agencies which the pools and the UGG have formed and which it is hoped will play an active part in the selling world. This government has not mentioned anything about this. There are many things which could be done which would be far more effective in helping the farmer than the three pieces of legislation the minister has brought in. Each piece of legislation creates more and more difficulty for the farmer in his attempt to remain in business.
The Canadian Wheat Board has been one of the major tools in assisting the farmer in respect of marketing his grain in the past number of years. However, the system should be changed. It should be made more flexible. The Canadian Wheat Board should be made more of a market-oriented board for Canada rather than a board which just controls the amount of grain produced by the farmers. Another thing I should like to mention is that in respect of the pricing system of the Canadian Wheat Board there should also be some changes. Last fall, because of the inflexibility of the Canadian Wheat Board we saw a situation in which Canadian barley sold at least 20 cents a bushel less than it should have for over a period of nearly two months. Because of the corn blight

May 20, 1971

in the United States, the demand for feed grain in Europe and Japan increased. We made sales because we were removed from the pressure of the demand in the barley market. If barley, however, were under the Canadian Wheat Board the pricing system would be too rigid. The rapeseed growers are worried about the possibility of a similar situation developing in respect of rapeseed.
Rapeseed is in severe competition with other oil seeds. With the selling system we have today there is a demand for the product. We know the supply and we know the demand. The Canadian Wheat Board is aware of the supply situation. It knows how many million bushels are in the elevators across Canada, at the Lakehead, at Vancouver and at Churchill, but the board must be more sensitive to the demand. It knows the supply situation but sales cannot be made unless we have the two factors at work, supply and demand. The rapeseed producers fear, if rapeseed is placed under the Canadian Wheat Board, that because of the inflexibility of the board's structure there might be a tendency to hide the demand for their commodity. This commodity is in severe competition with other oil seeds. Surely every farmer in Western Canada knows this. Surely a person who comes from Saskatchewan University should know this because Saskatchewan University has done a great deal of work in developing various uses for rapeseed. They should be well aware that demand must be registered. Because of the structure of the Canadian Wheat Board there might be a slight tendency to hide the demand. Therefore there is a great reluctance on the part of the growers to have rapeseed come under the Canadian Wheat Board, with all the rigidity which is built into the system. I think perhaps this bill, along with the other two which are before the committee, will receive exhaustive study.
Before I conclude, may I say that this morning in the Agricultural Committee the spokesmen for the Canadian Wheat Board were very poorly prepared. When they were asked questions they did not have the ansnwers. They said that they really did not think the question were within the terms of reference of this bill and so on. It would seem to me

and I come back to where I started-when you have 46,675 farmers in default on payments in respect of cash advance loans, then the committee study should encompass the whole spectrum of farming. I have never seen the representatives of the Canadian Wheat Board appear before an Agriculture Committee as poorly prepared as they were this morning. I know these are capable men. Why then did we have this situation? It must have been because of pressure from the top to release only what had to be released and no more. That is what I believe. I believe there is this pressure because the government does not want to become involved in a big debate.

The Minister of Agriculture suggests a wrong interpretation as usual. I was at the committee and was questioning the witnesses. How can the minister say all the information available was given and there was no direction from the top when he was not there? He does not know what information was requested. He does not know what information was not available. At one time the annual report of the Canadian Wheat Board went before the Agriculture Committee and was given a thorough study section by section. This procedure has not been followed for the last two or three years. I wonder why. The Canadian Wheat Board hired a very able and capable writer. He can write and he can carry on a great public relations job for them. Surely, he should be able to write enough about what the Board is doing for the Canadian farmer. The minister can say that there was no direction from the top, but I am only trying to analyse why more information was not made available. As we get into the study of this bill and of the Grain Stabilization Act, all the facts must be laid on the table and must be made available. I was disappointed.
I have been a member of the Standing Committee on Agriculture for 13 years, and I was very disappointed. Officials of the Wheat Board have always been very able witnesses before that committee. They have always known their facts, and they always gave out their information clearly and freely. This morning nearly all the same men were there. I understand that the chairman is in the hospital, but I am not certain about that. However, his assistants were there. They have always been before the committee, but for some reason or other much of the information was not available. The minister said that enough pertinent information was available. That is his opinion, but surely before we pass the three bills all the information that is required regarding the operation of the Wheat Board and the sales that they are supposed to have made as well as those they have made should be made known.
In addition, the action the Canadian Wheat Board took to reduce the amount of grain in storage must be explained. I think the truth will come out that this was a direction from the top, a direction which resulted in empty elevators throughout western Canada and which forced farmers to store more grain on their farms, in this way depriving them of much ready cash. It seems to me that this Action will only force farmers off the land, and that is exactly what the government is doing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DETERMINATION OF PAYMENT FOR WHEAT-EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO FLAXSEED, RYE AND RAPESEED
speechtext:
I want to spend a few minutes making some remarks on Bill C-238. I will be brief as the House has had before it in the last few days several different farm bills and all of us have had

May 20, 1971
Canadian Wheat Board Act
an opportunity to express our thoughts. These bills will be before the House again.
The bill before us deals essentially with a whole series of matters. First of all, there is a series of housekeeping provisions on which I do not intend to comment. For example, the bill provides for the extension of the crop year. I think most of my constituents are pretty well unanimous on this provision. The bill also makes some alterations in terminology. It refers to Thunder Bay rather than to Port Arthur and Fort William. When I say housekeeping provisions I do not mean it in the negative sense, but a large part of the bill deals with housekeeping matters.
The main point about which I and many other members of the House are concerned relates to the provision which permits marketing of flax, rye and rapeseed under the Canadian Wheat Board. What we have essentially is enabling legislation. If the minister or the cabinet see fit to include these commodities under the Wheat Board at some time, they will do so. I should like to ask the minister when he rises to speak again why he does not move now to include these commodities under the Wheat Board. Why is he again at this time in the position of going half way and not all the way? Why is he just half pregnant? This is often all too typical of this government. They go a little way down the path but not all the way. This is another small example of their over-cautiousness and of the timidity of the minister.
My position on the matter is quite clear. I am in favour of the immediate inclusion of flax, rye and rapeseed under the Canadian Wheat Board. I know other members of my party suggested this on Monday when they spoke in the House. I am in favour of the orderly marketing of all grains by the Canadian Wheat Board, an agency that is responsible to the public and to the producers. This is what we must have if there is to be any type of income stability for the farmer. In this way, farm commodities will not be the subject of speculation on the market, as is the case at present. This is why I should like to see the minister move as rapidly as possible to include these three commodities under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board.
Why do I say this? First of all, to be very brief, the major farm organizations and farmers unions, the wheat pools in the three provinces, and the Federation of Agriculture have all agreed that these commodities should be included under the Canadian Wheat Board. Since 1935, our party has passed resolutions at several conventions recommending the inclusion of these grains under the Wheat Board. I know that my constituents and the farmers in my area are in favour of such a move. I believe that this is the type of action which we should take, and we should not be pussyfooting around delaying it.
I am all the more convinced that we should take this action when I look at who is against the inclusion of these commodities under the Wheat Board. I see that, for example, the private grain trade is against such action, and so is the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. The other day one of the members in the House quoted a letter from James Richardson and Sons, a newsletter which was sent
out on April 22. I do not have the letter here but I know that James Richardson and Sons are against the inclusion of these commodities under the Wheat Board. When I learn this, I am all the more convinced that we must do so immediately because companies, organizations and corporations such as this have been living off the farmers and exploiting them for all too many years. It is about time we did something about such exploitation. As I said, such organizations have been living off the farmers, but this is not their fault; it is only natural. They are private corporations, and their aim is to make the maximum amount of profit with the lowest amount of effort. Their aim is to have a handsome profit from the sale of grain and other commodities which the farmer raises or produces. This is why the government should take the lead now and should initiate action at this time to include these three products under the Wheat Board.
It is not only the Liberal government that is half pregnant. We also find that the Conservative party is in a similar position. On the other hand, some Conservative Members of Parliament are against the inclusion of these commodities under the Wheat Board. I think that this type of attitude is nothing but an extreme right wing attitude which hearkens back to the age of the dinosaur. It assumes that the farmer can go out on the open market and fight for himself. The other day the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) said that the government is committed to a policy of economic genocide against the small scale farmer. I think he is right. I think the government in forcing small scale farmers off the land. This is their announced intention.
If some Conservative members vote against a piece of legislation such as this, then it can be assumed that there is certainly Conservative complicity in working against the operators of small farms. They want us to move even faster to force these farmers off the land. The hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) and the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), the two former cabinet ministers, left the cabinet because they thought the government was too cautious and too conservative. Now, we have some Conservative members saying that the government is not conservative enough. I think this speaks for itself. This is not the direction in which we must move. We must move in the other direction so that the farmer will have some protection and some bargaining power when he goes out into world markets. He must not be left to cope with the vagaries of the speculative market, but must be given some kind of stability. I think the minister knows this.
The minister is from Saskatchewan. I know he has been in contact with farm organizations. I hope he will act upon their recommendations as soon as possible because it is his duty to lead the way and to bring these commodities under the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board. He should listen to these organizations, and listen to them before the end of this crop year. If he does not, then perhaps there is some validity to the suggestion of some hon. members that a plebiscite be held. But that plebiscite would be a foregone conclusion because farmers are in favour of this legislation.

The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) says that some of the organizations may not be in favour of it. If that is the case I suggest they are few and far between because most farmers are interested in strengthening the Wheat Board, and in orderly marketing. Of course, you do have people who are critical of some of the ways in which the Wheat Board acts. There are many who feel it should be more aggressive, that it should be permitted to sell grain in a much more vigorous way.
But this is not the fault of the Wheat Board. This is not the fault of the basic idea of the orderly marketing of grains. This is the fault of the government for not giving the Board enough money, enough leeway, and enough motivation to go out and pursue better markets. If these commodities are included under the Wheat Board there is a better chance of finding markets for them, and a much better chance of getting more stable prices for the farmers. After all, this is what we want. Since when did the private grain trade have the interests of the farmer at heart? When did they become the friend of the farmer? Their purpose is to make a profit, as large a profit as possible. This is why I urge the minister to act as soon as possible, and not leave the whole thing up in the air, as apparently is being done today. We must strengthen the Wheat Board, make it more vigorous, give it more power and influence. We must make it a more aggressive agency. This is what the overwhelming majority of farmers in western Canada want.
I do not want to repeat myself, Mr. Speaker, but I do want to say that western agriculture is in really serious danger today. Farmers are rapidly disappearing from the land. The net income of the farmer has gone down and his costs have gone up. If we do not do something soon to reverse this trend the small farms will disappear, we will have huge corporate impersonal farms; local towns will become ghost communities or remain just as service centres for the corporate farms. Just a few weeks ago the Dominion Bureau of Statistics showed that net farm income in Saskatchewan over the two year period from 1968 to 1970 fell by 56 per cent. This is a gigantic drop. It underlines the severity of the problem facing western agriculture. And it is not only the farmer who is suffering. The operators of small businesses are affected, the unemployed, and in fact the whole population. A drop in income of 56 per cent should make us all realize there is something drastically and fundamentally wrong.
The bill before us is only a small one, but it provides for a fundamental change that would give a little more stability to some suffering farmers in western Canada. I hope the minister acts as soon as possible to have rye, flax and rapeseed brought under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. Perhaps when he rises to reply he will elaborate a bit more, tell us that he intends to 24107-30
Canadian Wheat Board Act
make a thorough, in-depth study of the matter, and indicate what his final decision will be. I have put forward what I find to be the general position of most people I talk to in rural Saskatchewan, and that is the position of the farm organizations also. It is about time that the farmer did have some bargaining power. It is about time that the farmer did have some protection. This is one little piece of legislation that would help the farmer in contending with forces which he cannot control by himself.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DETERMINATION OF PAYMENT FOR WHEAT-EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO FLAXSEED, RYE AND RAPESEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to my neighbour from Yorkton as he recited the dire conditions in which many western communities find themselves. He stated that there is a need for greater income in western Canada. He pointed out that some rural communities were depleted, and with all of this I agree entirely. I think he presented a good case showing there was a need for effective means to increase the income of the western farmers, and he also mentioned the needs of western businessmen.
Three of the major crops that western producers have been selling, wheat, oats and barley, have been under the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board for some time. Mr. Speaker, it was the dynamic salesmanship of the Wheat Board that piled up the huge surpluses that we now have, and so the hon. member for Yorkton immediately refutes his own argument when he says we should put other grains under the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board. Even though the Wheat Board was not able to handle the situation with regard to wheat, oats and barley, the hon. member suggests that it be given control over three more grains. And he suggests that then we will have orderly marketing.
We have had orderly marketing, Mr. Speaker. As a result we have stacked our surpluses up so neatly and so high that the whole world can see them. It doesn't matter where you stand, you can see piles of wheat in Canada.

speechtext: Do you want to abolish the Wheat Board?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DETERMINATION OF PAYMENT FOR WHEAT-EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO FLAXSEED, RYE AND RAPESEED
speechtext:
I did not suggest that I wanted to abolish the Wheat Board, but I do not want it burdened with any more commodities since it has indicated it cannot handle the three commodities already under its control.
The one salvation western farmers have had was the fact that rapeseed and flaxseed were outside the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board. It was not the Wheat Board's salesmanship that sold those commodities, to the point that we had no more rapeseed left to sell. In fact we had to increase our production of rapeseed, and we hope to increase it again. It was not the Wheat Board that did the work for us. It was the Rapeseed Association and the private trade which did the effective work. The hon. member may chastise the private trade, and suggest that it is living off the farmers, but I do not know how an elevator system can be maintained without deductions collected from the producer. As a producer I realize that, and what concerns me is that the elevator system may disappear if these other three grains come under the

May 20, 1971
Canadian Wheat Board Act
jurisdiction of the Wheat Board because then the absolute control will be in the hands of that board, which ultimately means in the hands of the government.
I have before me the report of the Canadian Grain Marketing Committee submitted to the Canadian Wheat Board, and on page 6 I read that in the year 1969-70 Canada's percentage of the world wheat carry-over was 39.4. At the same time, of the world wheat acreage in production, Canada has only 4.9 per cent-5 per cent of the total production acreage in the world and 40 per cent of the surplus. And wheat was handled by the Wheat Board, if you please! Do hon. members want a similar situation to occur with regard to rapeseed? As a producer I believe in pooling many things but at the moment I do not believe that rapeseed should be included. Now that somebody else has done the work the Wheat Board wants to move in. This is typical socialist philosophy, as I know very well having lived under it. They do not want a man to think for himself nor do they want the individual to make a profit. Personally, I do not mind anybody making a profit, though I may mind the margin of profit. I am more concerned about the man who is losing money because we know that profit is a great incentive.
The rapeseed industry is in competition with peanut oil, soya bean oil, coconut oil-you name it and we have it, but we have managed to sell our rapeseed. Now, the Wheat Board says it has the answer. It did not have the answer when we had a surplus of wheat. And what is the situation in regard to feed grain? In a newspaper report of a paper written by Dr. George R. Winter of the University of British Columbia there is the following statement:
Canada's share of world exports has fallen from nearly 30 per cent in 1963 (and a huge 40 per cent in war years) to less than 20 per cent in the last two years. On the other hand, Dr. Winter said, "We have only 3 per cent of world feed grain exports."
Only 3 per cent of world feed grain exports, Mr. Speaker! What about barley and oats? When we had a surplus of barley, farmers were moving it across provincial borders and doing everything to save themselves because the Wheat Board was not moving it. Then, there was a corn blight in the United States, although the Wheat Board did not realize this, and suddenly there was a windfall. However, the board sold barley at reduced prices. Before the Board caught on to what had happened they had committed themselves so far ahead at these reduced prices that the minister has had to up the ante by ten cents this year in order to encourage the delivery of barley. He established it low enough at first to protect himself, but now he has to deliver and he cannot do it because the farmers will not deliver at the reduced price. The minister has had to increase the price. That is the way the Wheat Board manipulates things; they up the ante and the elevators do not spot the cars. How do you get your barley into the elevator? There is no way you can operate a system that is obviously inefficient.

I believe that thorough discussion of this matter can only be obtained through the holding of a plebiscite. Let the trade explain its position if these profits are being made. However, at the same time we have to explain why we want rapeseed excluded. The farmers will be the judges. If the minister has any dilemma about who should participate in the plebiscite I suggest that any producer who has interested himself in the production of rapeseed over the last 10 or 20 years should be given a vote. I do not say every permit holder should be given a vote because if a permit holder were interested in producing he had the opportunity to do so over the years. Of course, he may be interested in the future, but then I may be interested in something else in the future. If you have a plebiscite of egg producers you only give a vote to those producers, not to the men who grow the grain that feeds the chickens that lay the eggs. The man who produces the particular grain which is the subject of the plebiscite should be the judge because he knows the situation.
The argument has been made that you need a pooling system because of the necessity to make long term sales. I reject that argument, Mr. Speaker, because we have a pooling arrangement in other commodities and it has not necessarily given us long term sales. In cases where it has, we have probably found out that some of the terms written in were not to our advantage. I can remember the U.K. agreement, a pooling arrangement which cost us $600 million. Western Canada was reeling for ten years after that and it was not just the farmer who lost, it was the whole western economy. When the rest of the world was making money we lost $600 million.
This question of averaging is an interesting one. If sales in the fall are low, then the quota itself establishes the price. You can only sell so much. For example, last fall we had some sales at $2.39 a bushel and then when the quota came up in January, we had some sales at $2.68 a bushel. There was a pooling effect, therefore, but there was no quota. The farmer is, therefore, necessarily restricted by the quota. The quota itself is a mechanism that will, in effect, balance off the average. That is what the Canadian Wheat Board is all about; it is a pooling arrangement, an averaging of prices through the mechanism of the quota.
We are told the pooling effect is needed for long term sales. But what is to stop an agency of the government or the Wheat Board from going into the world to find a market? They could ask potential buyers, "How much do you need and how much will you pay?" Then, they could come back to the producer and say, "We have a potential sale for X number of bushels, will you produce it at such and such a price?" The farmer could then be the judge and enter into a contract or take his chance elsewhere. This could be done right now. If they have their supersalesmen sitting waiting for the starting bell then I say to them, go to it. We have situations at the moment where, because of their yearly requirements, some processors guarantee the farmer a certain price, then work out the

May 20, 1971

final details later. As a matter of fact, sometimes the processors give the producers an advance. This method is competitive and it works. It is the old auction mart method-"How much will you offer?" Many of us have been to auction marts and some of us have been sucked in on occasion, but there is nothing wrong with that method of selling. You establish a price; the buyer looks at the block which is for sale and says, "I do not have to hurry; I can pick up the goods whenever I am ready." As I said before, we were not indebted to the super-salesmanship of the Wheat Board.
I have a little clipping from the Country Guide in my hand. It is about one year old, but the article I wish to read is still very good. It would be worth the while of my socialist friends to my left to read it, study it and analyse it to see what can be done when people work for themselves independently, inspired by one thing only, the knowledge that they have a good commodity for sale. The rapeseed growers did not get the government to sell their rapeseed. Some people say to the government, "You must sell our product for us because you have the funds." Then, when the government does not sell enough those people raise Cain. That is done oflen enough, and you cannot lose your argument if you blame the government for your ills. My socialist friends have a lot to learn.
I am a producer of rapeseed and I have done fairly well. The only thing that kept my farm from going bankrupt was rapeseed; rapeseed sales saved us. We were able to pay our bills because we sold our rapeseed through private trading.

The association sent out teams of skilled commodity traders and research scientists to find new markets and prove the value of rapeseed and rapeseed products. It promoted rapeseed oil to consumers in Western Canada and it introduced it to home economist and dieticians in Eastern Canadian universities and institutions.
It published a cookbook in two languages and an animal nutritionist's manual in three. It organized leading plant breeders, animal nutritionists and oil chemists into research teams to develop better varieties and products.
The article goes on to mention the activities of the rapeseed association:
Its first trade mission went to Japan in May, 1968, J. M. Bell, University of Saskatchewan animal scientist, and Dr. R. K. Downey, oilseeds researcher, went along to explain to Japanese scientists the merits of rapeseed and rapeseed meal, and to help set up feeding trials there.

'It was a breakthrough,'... 'If rapeseed meal were to make up only 2% of formula feeds, Japan's need for rapeseed would be doubled.'
The Japanese need for rapeseed would be doubled if rapeseed meal, as the article points out, were to make up only 2 per cent of formula feeds. That article shows how rapeseed was sold. It was not sold through government intervention. People sold it by doing something for themselves. It was not the government or the Wheat Board that made those sales. The people who grew rapeseed paid a dollar or two into the association to create a fund and used that money to find a market for rapeseed. They knew what they wanted; they knew they had a good product and they knew it was needed by the rest of the world. Because it has been such a good crop everybody wants to get in on the act.
